displayQuote: Trust yourself. Create the kind of self that you will be happy to live with all your life

meta.title: Who really said "Trust yourself. Create the kind of self that you will be happy to live with all your life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Popularly pinned on Golda Meir, but the wording is documented under inspirational writer Foster C. McClellan — and appears in none of Meir's works.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Trust yourself. Create the kind of self that you will be happy to live with all your life'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Golda Meir across quote sites, but the line traces to writer Foster C. McClellan and is absent from every Meir source.

answer.label: Not Golda Meir — traced to Foster C. McClellan
answer.sourceLine: The oldest, most carefully edited quote references credit this full passage to Foster C. McClellan, an obscure American inspirational writer, sourced to a collection titled “Poor Man’s College.” No speech, book, interview, or letter by Golda Meir is known to contain it, and her Wikiquote page does not list it in any section — the Meir credit appears only on modern quote-aggregator sites with no source.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Trust yourself. Create the kind of self that you will be happy to live with all your life. Make the most of yourself by fanning the tiny, inner sparks of possibility into flames of achievement.
trail: The older, editorially curated Quotations Page credits the full passage to Foster C. McClellan, sourced to “Poor Man’s College” — not to Golda Meir.
Quotes.net likewise files the identical wording under Foster C. McClellan.
Golda Meir’s Wikiquote page does not contain the line in any section — sourced, disputed, or misattributed.
The Meir credit surfaces only on unsourced aggregators such as Goodreads, which warns its quotes are “not verified.”
source.excerptNote: The line almost always travels as this two-sentence pair; both halves are attributed together to Foster C. McClellan in the earliest careful references.

sourceLink.text: Foster C. McClellan on The Quotations Page

source.rightsHolder: Estate of Foster C. McClellan (or original publisher)
source.rightsNote: The wording is a 20th-century inspirational text — documented under Foster C. McClellan and clearly post-1931 — so it is treated as in-copyright. Because the exact first-publication date of “Poor Man’s College” is not established, the rights holder is given conservatively; a public-domain claim would be unsafe.

author.name: Foster C. McClellan
author.heading: About Foster C. McClellan
author.bio: Foster C. McClellan was a mid-20th-century American author of short inspirational and motivational pieces, including the booklet Thoughts for a Friend. His aphorisms circulated through gift booklets and syndicated inspirational columns such as the collection “Poor Man’s College,” which is where the earliest careful quote references place this line. He is little-documented today, which is precisely why his words drifted to a far more famous name.

misattribution.heading: Why Golda Meir gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s stock “strong-woman” inspirational quotes, and Golda Meir — Israel’s formidable prime minister — is a magnet for exactly this kind of sourceless feel-good wisdom.

items.why: Credited to Meir across BrainyQuote, Goodreads, and PassItOn — none of which cite a Meir speech, book, or interview, and none of which predate the McClellan attribution.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-sourced trail leads to Foster C. McClellan and the collection “Poor Man’s College,” per the Quotations Page — not to Golda Meir, whose documented writings and sourced Wikiquote entry contain no trace of it.

context.heading: A borrowed voice
lead: The sentiment — self-trust as a lifelong project of character — is the standard fare of mid-century American inspirational booklets, and it reads nothing like Golda Meir’s actual documented voice, which was terse, political, and often bleak (“Pessimism is a luxury that a Jew can never allow himself”).

The migration is a textbook case: an aphorism from a forgotten writer attaches to a globally famous name, gains authority from that name, and then circulates faster than anyone stops to ask for a source.
context.pull: The oldest careful trail leads to Foster C. McClellan — not to Golda Meir.
